notes: WebSearch tool was already at its session-wide 200/200 quota before this scout's first call, so all planned `site:github.com` WebSearch queries failed outright. Substituted: (1) WebFetch on github.com/search HTML pages -> 429 rate-limited; (2) WebFetch on DuckDuckGo html endpoint -> CAPTCHA wall; (3) WebFetch on Bing -> returned garbled/irrelevant snippets that didn't respect the site: filter; (4) WebFetch on the unauthenticated GitHub REST search API (api.github.com/search/repositories) worked reliably and is what most of these candidates came from, plus direct WebFetch verification of specific repo pages. This means coverage here leans toward what GitHub's own relevance/star ranking surfaces for the query terms used, not a broad web crawl (no Kaggle/Zenodo/HuggingFace/blog-post pages could be searched this way) -- a re-run with a working WebSearch budget would likely surface pointer-to-external-host datasets (Zenodo GDIS, Kaggle wildfire/EM-DAT mirrors, HuggingFace disaster-tweet corpora) that this pass could not reach. Dead ends: no GitHub-native EM-DAT full-database mirror found (EM-DAT is licensed/gated at source; only client libraries and course-project extracts exist, mostly small samples of unclear vintage). No dedicated 'STR occupancy during hurricane/wildfire' dataset found on GitHub. FEMA NRI hits were mostly one-off student class projects, not raw data mirrors (NRI itself is a FEMA-hosted download, not on GitHub). Most 'wildfire perimeter' and 'FIRMS' hits are live-monitoring/visualization tools built to hit NIFC/FIRMS APIs at query time rather than stored historical datasets -- catalogued as method, not stored data. Worth another scout pass once WebSearch quota resets, focused specifically on Kaggle/Zenodo pages for: Maui/Lahaina fire economic-impact studies, Gulf Coast/Florida hurricane tourism-recovery panels, and EM-DAT CSV re-hosts.

candidates.name: fema-disaster-declarations-summaries
candidates.what_it_holds: Automated mirror of OpenFEMA's 'Disaster Declarations Summaries V2' dataset via AWS Data Exchange: every federally declared disaster (major disaster, fire management, emergency declarations) from 1953 onward, county-level from 1964 onward, 22 fields (declaration string, disaster number, state/county FIPS, incident type, declaration date, IA/PA/HM program flags). CSV/JSON/JSONA, updated daily against FEMA's NEMIS system.
candidates.why_useful: Directly addresses gap #11 (events/shocks: hurricanes/wildfires) and gap #12-adjacent regulatory/declaration tracking; gives a clean county x date x incident-type panel to flag which weeks/markets in the Inside Airbnb 13-city / 123-market panels sat inside a federal disaster window (Maui wildfire, LA fires, Gulf hurricanes) for tourism-shock event studies.
candidates.size_hint: full historical disaster-declaration table, tens of thousands of rows
candidates.license: not explicit in repo; underlying data is FEMA/OpenFEMA public domain
candidates.last_activity: 2021-06-23 (repo scaffold; data refreshed via AWS Data Exchange subscription rather than repo commits)

candidates.name: fema-mcp-server
candidates.what_it_holds: MCP server / client that queries FEMA disaster declarations, public-assistance grants, individual housing-assistance data, and NFIP flood-insurance claims through FEMA's live OpenFEMA API.
candidates.why_useful: One-command programmatic pull of the same OpenFEMA declaration + assistance + NFIP-claims data as the rearc mirror, but live and queryable, including NFIP flood claims which give a dollar-loss proxy per county/disaster not in the plain declarations file.
candidates.time_coverage: current OpenFEMA API coverage, historical since NEMIS (1998) plus back-filled declarations

candidates.name: firedpy
candidates.what_it_holds: Python CLI (Earth Lab, CU Boulder) that classifies individual wildfire events from the MODIS Collection 6.1 Burned Area Product (MCD64A1) into discrete fire-event polygons (event-level and optional daily-expansion perimeters), output as GeoPackage/Shapefile plus attribute tables. Global via MODIS tiles; pre-built extracts available per US state/country/continent. Coverage November 2000 - December 2024 (v2.0, Oct 2024 release extends some regions to 2025).
candidates.why_useful: Gives reproducible, dated wildfire-perimeter polygons (not just point hotspots) for any US state or country -- usable to build a 'was market X inside an active/recent fire perimeter' flag for California, Hawaii (Maui) and other Inside Airbnb markets, filling gap #11 with actual geometry rather than a news list.
candidates.size_hint: generates shapefiles/GeoPackages per region; pre-built US-state extracts sized in the 10s-100s of MB

candidates.name: datacenters-wildfires
candidates.what_it_holds: Interactive map + underlying data pull of US historical wildfire perimeters sourced from NIFC/WFIGS (National Interagency Fire Center Wildland Fire Interagency Geospatial Services), covering 2016 through September 2026.
candidates.why_useful: A recent, actively updated (pushed 2026-09-10) mirror/consumer of the authoritative US wildfire-perimeter feed (NIFC/WFIGS) reaching into 2026, i.e. covers the LA fires (Jan 2025) and any 2026 events relevant to the pitch window.
candidates.size_hint: not stated; built on NIFC/WFIGS perimeter polygons

candidates.name: nasa-wildfires
candidates.what_it_holds: LA Times Data Desk's Python tool to download wildfire hotspot detections from NASA satellites via FIRMS (MODIS/VIIRS), returning point-level fire-detection data with timestamps and confidence.
candidates.why_useful: A well-maintained (34 stars), newsroom-grade one-command puller for near-real-time and historical FIRMS hotspot data -- lower-fidelity than perimeter polygons but easy to script for any market/date range, including Hawaii and Southern California.
candidates.time_coverage: current NASA FIRMS archive (2000-present for MODIS, 2012-present VIIRS)
candidates.license: not stated (LA Times Data Desk open-source tools are typically MIT/permissive)

candidates.name: hurricaneexposuredata
candidates.what_it_holds: R data package with hazard-based exposure data (storm-level rain and wind exposure) for every US county within the Atlantic-basin hurricane-affected region, keyed to specific historical tropical-storm events; companion to the `hurricaneexposure` toolkit (rOpenSci-affiliated) which layers on visualization/analysis functions.
candidates.why_useful: County-level, storm-by-storm exposure intensity (not just track lines) lets you quantify how directly a given Inside Airbnb market (e.g. Florida, Gulf Coast, coastal NC/SC) was hit by a named storm -- useful for a hurricane-shock control variable in nights/ADR regressions, addressing gap #11.
candidates.time_coverage: historical tropical storms through package's last data refresh (package built off HURDAT2 vintages)
candidates.size_hint: 13 stars, 6 forks, 102 commits; R package data/ directory
candidates.license: not explicitly stated in fetched excerpt (rOpenSci packages are typically MIT/GPL)
candidates.last_activity: not shown in fetch excerpt; rOpenSci-reviewed package, periodically maintained

candidates.name: ibtracs
candidates.what_it_holds: Python API/wrapper for interfacing with NOAA's IBTrACS (International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship) global tropical-cyclone best-track dataset -- position, intensity, and metadata for every tracked tropical cyclone worldwide since ~1841 (satellite-era reliable from ~1980s).
candidates.why_useful: Global coverage (not just Atlantic/HURDAT2) matters for APAC typhoon exposure (Japan, Thailand, Philippines -- gap #7 APAC travel volume interacts with typhoon season) and for a global, not just US, hurricane/typhoon shock variable.
candidates.time_coverage: ~1841-present (reliable satellite era ~1980s-present), updated as NOAA IBTrACS releases new versions
candidates.size_hint: wrapper around NOAA's canonical IBTrACS CSV/NetCDF files (~10s of MB)

candidates.name: IBTrACS
candidates.what_it_holds: Repository directly committing IBTrACS CSV files (global tropical cyclone best-track data) rather than just a client wrapper.
candidates.why_useful: A committed, version-controlled copy of IBTrACS CSVs on GitHub -- easier to pin/point-in-time than always pulling live from NOAA, useful if the team wants a frozen vintage for backtesting hurricane-season effects.
candidates.time_coverage: IBTrACS full historical record as of repo's last commit
candidates.size_hint: CSV files, tens of MB typical for full IBTrACS

candidates.name: HURDAT2_processor
candidates.what_it_holds: Python script converting NOAA's Atlantic hurricane database (HURDAT2) raw fixed-width text format into a clean pandas dataframe / CSV (storm id, name, date/time, lat/lon, max wind, pressure, per 6-hourly fix).
candidates.why_useful: A simple, no-dependency way to get HURDAT2 (the standard official Atlantic-basin storm-track record used by NHC) into an analysis-ready CSV without hand-parsing the NOAA text format, directly supporting Gulf/Atlantic hurricane-season event studies (gap #11).
candidates.size_hint: single script + resulting CSV of a few MB

candidates.name: python-aio-georss-gdacs
candidates.what_it_holds: Async Python client for the Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System (GDACS) GeoRSS feed -- real-time and near-term-historical alerts for earthquakes, tropical cyclones, floods, volcanoes, droughts, and wildfires worldwide, each with a severity/alert-level score.
candidates.why_useful: GDACS gives a single cross-hazard, cross-country severity feed (not just US-only like FEMA) -- useful as a lightweight global disaster-shock indicator across APAC/LatAm/EMEA markets that FEMA/NIFC/HURDAT2 don't cover, complementing gap #11 outside the US.
candidates.time_coverage: live feed; GDACS itself archives alerts back to the mid-2000s on its own site
candidates.license: not stated (exxamalte's georss packages are typically Apache-2.0)

candidates.name: emdatr
candidates.what_it_holds: R package (CRAN mirror) 'Global disaster losses from the EM-DAT database' -- functions to load/process EM-DAT (CRED Université catholique de Louvain) global natural-disaster loss records (deaths, affected population, damage estimates) by country/year/disaster-type.
candidates.why_useful: Direct EM-DAT tooling named in the theme's own keyword hints; EM-DAT itself is licensed/registration-gated at source (no full open GitHub mirror was found), so this is the closest thing to a reusable open client, though the package itself is old (2015) and would need a fresh EM-DAT export to be useful today.
candidates.time_coverage: EM-DAT coverage as of package's last CRAN sync (~2015); underlying EM-DAT goes back to 1900
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: none held; EM-DAT itself not otherwise in our holdings

candidates.name: fema-disaster-information
candidates.what_it_holds: Analysis repo combining FEMA Disaster Declarations and Public Assistance data, with committed extracts/notebooks (per repo description: 'FEMA Disaster Declarations and Public Assistance Data Analysis').
candidates.why_useful: Secondary/smaller alternative to the rearc-data mirror; worth a quick look if that one's AWS Data Exchange dependency is inconvenient, since Public Assistance $ amounts by disaster give a rough severity/dollar-cost proxy per event.
candidates.time_coverage: not specified precisely; likely recent-decade OpenFEMA extract
candidates.size_hint: 5 stars; notebook + data files, scale unclear
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: overlaps rearc-data/fema-disaster-declarations-summaries (candidate above), which is the more authoritative/automated version

candidates.name: perimeter
candidates.what_it_holds: Coverage/measurement code over California's wildfire perimeter datasets sourced from FRAP (Fire and Resource Assessment Program) and CAL FIRE -- California's own authoritative historical wildfire-perimeter record (predates and complements NIFC/WFIGS).
candidates.why_useful: CAL FIRE/FRAP is the longest-running state-level wildfire perimeter archive (decades of California fires) -- useful specifically for the LA and broader California Inside Airbnb markets named in the theme brief.
candidates.time_coverage: CAL FIRE FRAP historical archive (multi-decade, exact span not confirmed from listing alone)

candidates.name: wildfire-perimeters
candidates.what_it_holds: Showcase app exploring STAC (SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog) fire-event data hosted by NASA's VEDA (Visualization, Exploration, and Data Analysis) platform -- points to VEDA's own fire-event STAC collections rather than committing data itself.
candidates.why_useful: Points to NASA VEDA's STAC fire-event catalog, a modern queryable geospatial index of US fire events that could be pulled directly (via STAC API) for perimeter + date without needing firedpy's local MODIS processing.
candidates.time_coverage: per VEDA's own fire-event STAC catalog coverage
candidates.size_hint: showcase app; data lives on NASA VEDA (https://openveda.cloud)
